newsitem.title: USA: CFTC mulls pilot program for U.S. ag trade options.
newsitem.headline: CFTC mulls pilot program for U.S. ag trade options.

text.p: A three-year pilot program with regulatory oversight is the best way to find out the impact of lifting a longstanding ban on agricultural trade options, Commodity Futures Trading Commission chairwoman Brooksley Born said on Wednesday.

"I personally would feel... that a pilot program would be the appropriate way to introduce this and see how it would do," Born told a House Agriculture subcommittee hearing. "I would think something like three years would be appropriate with careful regulatory scrutiny if we decided to go that way."

Thursday marks the end of the public comment period on the CFTC's notice of a proposed rulemaking that would lift the 61-year-old ban. After reviewing the comments, the CFTC will decide whether to formally propose lifting the ban.
The CFTC held two hearings earlier this month in Memphis, Tenn. and Bloomington, Ill. to hear the views of agricultural groups and producers.

Born also said it was "unrealistic" to expect the CFTC to complete any potential rulemaking to lift the ban by October. CFTC Commissioner Joe Dial, a supporter of ag trade options, had previously said he hoped the agency would act by then to make the risk management tool available to farmers preparing for the next planting season.
Although several grain, cotton and other producer groups have said they want to use ag trade options, the the two biggest U.S. futures exchanges were divided on the issue.

The Chicago Mercantile Exchange said it opposed making ag trade options available because the same risk management results can be achieved through exchange-traded instruments, but the Chicago Board of Trade said it would support a pilot program with CFTC reporting requirements.

"The CFTC is ill-equipped to monitor or enforce the sale and use of off-exchange instruments," John Sandner, chairman of the CME, told the House panel. "It is not reasonable to assume that the average farmer, to whom these options will be marketed, possesses the same degree of financial sophistication as the participants in the financial over-the-counter market."
He pointed to the problems last year with hedge-to-arrive contracts used by some farmers and grain elevators. Those off-exchange contracts resulted in financial losses and lawsuits, he said.

The CME is developing so-called "flex options" for its live cattle, lean hogs, feeder cattle and pork bellies contracts, patterned after the CME's flex options for equity index markets, he said. Flex options allow a user to create a customized option by specifying the expiration date, strike price and American or European style to match his or her specific needs.

With flex options, traders on the floor take the customer's specifications into consideration and calculate an appropriate premium, Sandner said. "Competition among floor traders assures that the best quote is offered to the hedger, and the hedger is then free to accept or decline that quote."
David Lehman, group manager of commodity products for the CBOT, said a pilot program would be an important safeguard for producers.

"Restricting the instruments allowed for the first three years to crop revenue products only will provide relief to the market segment which has the greatest need for additional flexible risk management tools," Lehman told the panel. "This approach would also provide valuable information to USDA and Congress on the potential for reducing government subsidies for the crop insurance and crop revenue programs."

The American Farm Bureau Federation said it supported lifting the ban, but asked the CFTC to establish minimum financial standards for writers of ag trade options, to limit the size of transactions and to restrict option vendors to commercial entities directly involved in the handling or use of the commodity.

Ag trade options would allow a farmer to buy an option from a local elevator to sell the farm's anticipated production of corn or other commodity at a certain price. The off-exchange options give producers and processors the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell a commodity at a certain price.
